subtype: Approach: inviting dissent and choosing by criteria [Revision]
passage: After our model failed, I changed how we chose the next design. I asked Preeti and each of the other three to say one concern about every idea, out loud, before any vote. At first it felt awkward. Preeti said the second idea needed glue that took two days to dry. Someone else said the tower might not fit through the classroom door. Then we scored each idea from one to five on cost, time and whether it could really be built. The confident idea, the one I had loved, got a low score on feasibility, which surprised me. The plainest idea won. It was not exciting, but it stood up at the test. I'm Sharmila, and I've learned to ask before I decide.

qa.q: How did the group score each idea?
qa.a: They scored each idea from one to five on cost, time and whether it could really be built.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when the loved idea scored low?
qa.a: Sharmila was surprised and a little disappointed, since Sharmila had loved that idea.

qa.q: What could Sharmila add for the next decision, and why?
qa.a: Sharmila could ask a teacher to review the shortlist before the final vote, because an outside view catches problems the group cannot see.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about being asked for a concern?
qa.a: Preeti probably felt relieved to be invited to speak, since the concern about glue drying time was heard and used.

grounding: After the failure, the leader asks each member to state one concern and scores ideas on cost, time and feasibility, so the next decision uses evidence rather than confidence.
